name: broadcom
product: CA ACF2 and CA Top Secret

corpus.note: Measured 2026-09-21 over 127 public GitHub COBOL repositories, 558,281 files, with diag/measure-rules.mjs --packs. Read the denominator before the number: every rule in this pack is JCL-scoped, and only 45 of the 127 repositories contain any JCL at all. WHAT THIS DOES AND DOES NOT SHOW. It shows these rules are not broadly noisy - they do not fire on ordinary COBOL and JCL. It does not show they are quiet where they would actually run, because a public corpus of teaching material, vendor demos and tooling contains essentially no estate running this product. A rule that cannot fire for want of the product is not the same as a rule that sees the product and stays quiet, and this measurement cannot tell those apart. The practitioner review is still the half that would.

validation._note: Two different questions. A corpus measurement over public COBOL repositories tells you how often these rules fire, which is their noise. It cannot tell you whether the risk statements are true: if the claim about GSO records is wrong, a thousand repositories will report it quietly and wrongly. Fill corpus with {repositories, firedOn, perRule} from diag/measure-rules.mjs; fill practitioner with {by, date, note} when someone who has administered the product has read it.

source: CA ACF2 and CA Top Secret command references. Some are behind a Broadcom support login; a customer who runs the product can supply theirs.
coverage: Logonid and ACID administration, resource rule maintenance, and global option changes. Not covered: reporting utilities, database maintenance, or anything whose risk depends on the installation's own rule set.

rules.rationale: An INSERT while the session is in logonid maintenance mode creates a logonid. The mode matters: without it this matches SQL INSERT INTO, which a corpus measurement over 125 repositories found 322 times. A logonid created from a job in a repository is a credential whose existence is decided by whoever can commit.
rules.remedy: Create logonids through the ACF2 administration process the security team owns, not from a job in this repository. Where batch maintenance must stay, keep the job where only security administrators can change it.

rules.risk: alters a logonid, including its privileges
rules.rationale: CHANGE against a logonid alters its attributes. The privileged attributes here are the ones that matter, and the same statement carries both ordinary and privileged changes.
rules.remedy: Make logonid changes through the security team's administration process rather than from a committed job, and have each privileged attribute a change sets approved before it is applied.

rules.rationale: Access rule maintenance decides who may reach which dataset or resource. Changing it from a job means the access model is edited by whoever can edit the repository.
rules.remedy: Maintain access rule sets through the security team's change process, not from an application job. Where rules are kept as source, keep that source where only security administrators can change it.

rules.rationale: GSO records are installation-wide security options. A change here affects every user and every resource at once, which makes it the highest-value single statement in the product.
rules.remedy: Change GSO records only through the security team's controlled change process, never from an application job.
steps: Remove the SET CONTROL(GSO) maintenance from the job.
Raise the option change with the security team, who make it through their own change process.
Check the job library's history for earlier GSO changes run from it, and confirm each one with the security team.

rules.rationale: TSS CREATE defines a new accessor identity. As with an ACF2 logonid, an identity created from a committed job is decided by whoever can commit.
rules.remedy: Create ACIDs through the Top Secret administration process the security team owns, not from a job in this repository.

rules.rationale: TSS PERMIT grants an ACID access to a resource. It is the statement that turns an identity into an authorisation, and it is the one an attacker most wants to be able to issue.
rules.remedy: Grant access through the security team's request and approval process, not from a committed job. Where a grant must be scripted, keep the script where only security administrators can change it.

rules.risk: grants a bypassing or master-level attribute
rules.rationale: The attributes matched here remove or bypass normal validation. An ACID carrying one of them is outside the controls every other identity is subject to, which is a different class of finding from an ordinary grant.
rules.remedy: Remove the bypassing or master-level attribute from the job. Grant such an attribute only through the security team's controlled process, to a named identity, and review who holds it.
steps: Remove the TSS ADDTO that grants the attribute from the job.
List the ACIDs that hold the attribute now, and confirm each one with the security team.
Have the security team grant any attribute still needed through their own process.

rules.risk: removes an identity or an authorisation
rules.rationale: Removing access from a job is less immediately dangerous than granting it, and it is still the security model being edited from a repository. It is listed so the route is visible, at a severity that says which way round it is.
rules.remedy: Remove access through the security team's administration process rather than from an application job, so the change is approved and recorded where the rest of the security model is.
